fact_text: The refinery upgrade policy is framed as import substitution: cleaner local refining means fewer finished petrol and diesel imports, keeping the price gap between products and crude at home.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Pakistan Refinery Policy 2026 | Which Refinery Has the Strongest Upgrade Plan?' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst expects most of the refinery upgrade capital to arrive as foreign direct investment, which would put less pressure on Pakistan's foreign exchange reserves.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Pakistan Refinery Policy 2026 | Which Refinery Has the Strongest Upgrade Plan?' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The budget waived sales tax on machinery imported for refinery upgrades, which improves the economics of the upgrade projects.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Pakistan Refinery Policy 2026 | Which Refinery Has the Strongest Upgrade Plan?' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The policy pays a bigger incentive to refiners that finish the upgrade quickly, within about three years; full upgrades are otherwise expected to take three to five years.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Pakistan Refinery Policy 2026 | Which Refinery Has the Strongest Upgrade Plan?' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The policy gives refiners and government more certainty: the upgrade terms are meant to hold for a couple of years after signing, so neither side changes them soon after.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Pakistan Refinery Policy 2026 | Which Refinery Has the Strongest Upgrade Plan?' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The government's share of upgrade investment is recovered through a deemed duty levied on diesel and petrol, so the incentive is funded from fuel duties rather than from the refiner's own cash.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Pakistan Refinery Policy 2026 | Which Refinery Has the Strongest Upgrade Plan?' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: During supply shocks such as the US-Iran conflict, refining margins spike and government struggles to keep fuel supplied, which pushed the upgrade policy through.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Pakistan Refinery Policy 2026 | Which Refinery Has the Strongest Upgrade Plan?' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Upgrade savings come from four sources: less furnace oil output, a richer petrol and diesel mix, lower chemical use, and no penalties for fuel that is not Euro-5 compliant.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Pakistan Refinery Policy 2026 | Which Refinery Has the Strongest Upgrade Plan?' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Furnace oil sells at a deep discount to crude while petrol and diesel trade at a premium, so shifting output from furnace oil into light products widens the refiner's spread.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Pakistan Refinery Policy 2026 | Which Refinery Has the Strongest Upgrade Plan?' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: To size the product-mix gain, multiply the price spread per barrel by the share of output shifted, then by daily throughput and by operating days in the year.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Pakistan Refinery Policy 2026 | Which Refinery Has the Strongest Upgrade Plan?' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Euro-5 and Ron 92 penalties can be checked in the revenue section of a refiner's annual or nine-month report, then annualised to size the savings from avoiding them.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Pakistan Refinery Policy 2026 | Which Refinery Has the Strongest Upgrade Plan?' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Refineries use heavy amounts of chemicals to optimise output from the current mix; the analyst expects chemical use to fall substantially once the upgrade favours petrol and diesel.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Pakistan Refinery Policy 2026 | Which Refinery Has the Strongest Upgrade Plan?' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Refineries have run below capacity because surplus furnace oil is sold at a loss; cutting furnace oil output lets plants run closer to full throughput.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Pakistan Refinery Policy 2026 | Which Refinery Has the Strongest Upgrade Plan?' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Local furnace oil demand is well below domestic output, so surplus furnace oil must be exported, which adds transport cost and a weaker realised price.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Pakistan Refinery Policy 2026 | Which Refinery Has the Strongest Upgrade Plan?' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: GRM, the gross refining margin, is the spread of petrol and diesel prices over crude oil, and it is set internationally rather than locally.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Pakistan Refinery Policy 2026 | Which Refinery Has the Strongest Upgrade Plan?' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: High refining margins let refiners fund upgrades from profit instead of new debt, so whether GRMs stay high over the next few quarters is a key input to the upgrade thesis.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Pakistan Refinery Policy 2026 | Which Refinery Has the Strongest Upgrade Plan?' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst's method is to estimate the extra profit an upgrade adds, compute the return on that investment, and then judge whether the current price justifies it.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Pakistan Refinery Policy 2026 | Which Refinery Has the Strongest Upgrade Plan?' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: A refiner's share price can already reflect part of a large announced upgrade, but the new capital may be raised through debt or a rights issue, so the price must be checked against that dilution.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Pakistan Refinery Policy 2026 | Which Refinery Has the Strongest Upgrade Plan?' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The climate finance facility carries a levy on furnace oil; the analyst argues that furnace oil is an industrial fuel and should face an industrial levy rather than a petroleum-product levy.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Pakistan Refinery Policy 2026 | Which Refinery Has the Strongest Upgrade Plan?' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Furnace oil is an industrial fuel, not a transport fuel, so it is not used in cars or bikes and its pricing and levy differ from petrol and diesel.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Pakistan Refinery Policy 2026 | Which Refinery Has the Strongest Upgrade Plan?' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: National Refinery has a nameplate capacity of about 55,000 to 60,000 barrels per day, but runs below it because furnace oil losses limit how hard the plant is pushed.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Pakistan Refinery Policy 2026 | Which Refinery Has the Strongest Upgrade Plan?' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst treats National Refinery as an upgrade play: converting furnace oil into diesel and petrol could lift throughput and profit, and part of that future profit may already sit in the share price.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Pakistan Refinery Policy 2026 | Which Refinery Has the Strongest Upgrade Plan?' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: A faster upgrade earns a larger government incentive, so the speed of National Refinery's upgrade programme is a catalyst the analyst watches.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Pakistan Refinery Policy 2026 | Which Refinery Has the Strongest Upgrade Plan?' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Government incentives fund about 20 to 22% of National Refinery's upgrade investment, with the company funding the rest of the capex, which the analyst treats as the basis for upgrade returns.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Pakistan Refinery Policy 2026 | Which Refinery Has the Strongest Upgrade Plan?' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Budget 2026 cut the super tax, which the analyst said lifts listed companies' profits and supports the market outlook.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Pakistan Refinery Policy 2026 | Which Refinery Has the Strongest Upgrade Plan?' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: After the 2025 India-Pakistan conflict, Pakistan's geopolitical position improved and interest rates fell; the market moved sideways in early 2025 before a strong rally from July 2025.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Pakistan Refinery Policy 2026 | Which Refinery Has the Strongest Upgrade Plan?' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst expects a similar sequence to repeat in the second half of 2026, since a sideways phase has ended and lower super tax is lifting company profits.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Pakistan Refinery Policy 2026 | Which Refinery Has the Strongest Upgrade Plan?' (YouTube transcript, undated)
